The '''Airbus A330neo''' ("neo" for "[[Re-engine|New Engine Option]]") is a [[wide-body airliner]] developed by [[Airbus]] from the original [[Airbus A330]] (now A330''ceo'' – "Current Engine Option").<ref name="Goold">{{cite web|url=https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2017-11-11/airbus-presents-updated-airliners-middle-east-carriers|title=Airbus Presents Updated Airliners to Middle East Carriers|last=Goold|first=Ian|date=11 November 2017|work=AIN Online|access-date=29 March 2020|quote=...Airbus had flown some planned improvements during a 130 flight-hour program with A330ceo (current engine option) MSN871...|archive-date=29 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329103954/https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2017-11-11/airbus-presents-updated-airliners-middle-east-carriers|url-status=live}}</ref> <!-- Studies --> A new version with modern engines comparable with those developed for the [[Boeing 787]] was called for by operators of the A330ceo. <!-- Launch --> It was launched on 14 July 2014 at the [[Farnborough Airshow]], promising 14% better [[Fuel economy in aircraft|fuel economy per seat]]. <!-- Engines --> It is exclusively powered by the [[Rolls-Royce Trent 7000]] which has double the [[bypass ratio]] of its [[Rolls-Royce Trent 700|predecessor]].

<!-- Variants -->Its two versions are based on the [[A330-200]] and -300: the -800 has a range of {{cvt|8,100|nmi|-1}} with 257 passengers while the -900 covers {{cvt|7,350|nmi|-1}} with 287 passengers.<!--testing/introduction--> The -900 made its [[maiden flight]] on 19 October 2017 and received its [[EASA]] type certificate on 26 September 2018; it was first delivered to [[TAP Air Portugal]] on 26 November 2018 and entered service on 15 December. The -800 made its first flight on 6 November 2018 and received EASA type certification on 13 February 2020; the first two -800s were delivered to [[Kuwait Airways]] on 29 October 2020 and entered service on 20 November.
<!--Orders & deliveries-->
{{As of|2026|10}}, a total of 559 A330neo family aircraft had been ordered by more than 30 customers, of which 203 aircraft had been delivered.

==Development==
===Studies===
[[File:Initial Airbus A350 concept.jpg|thumb|left|The initial [[A350]] concept, based on the [[A330#A330ceo|A330ceo]], before its redesign into the all-new A350XWB, was similar to what became the A330neo.]]

<!-- before 14 July 2014 -->
At the [[Boeing 787]] launch in 2004, Airbus' initial response was an improved A330. After negative feedback from airlines and [[lessor (leasing)|lessors]], the [[A350 XWB]] became a new design in 2006. After the [[A320neo]] launch in December 2010 and its commercial success, the largest airline of [[Malaysia]], [[AirAsia]] – an all-Airbus operator – asked Airbus to [[re-engine]] the A330.<ref name=Challenges2011/> New engines like the [[GEnx]] or [[Rolls-Royce Trent 1000]] developed for the 787 could offer a 12%–15% fuel burn improvement, and [[Blended winglets|sharklets]] at least 2%.<ref name=AI110718/>

Airbus sales chief [[John Leahy (executive)|John Leahy]]'s argument was that the lower purchase price of an A330 even without new engines make the economics of buying an A330 competitive at midrange routes with that of the Boeing 787.<ref name=AW120709/> An A330neo would accelerate the demise of the similarly sized [[A350-800]].<ref name=reuters140110/> Airbus also considered re-engining the [[Airbus A380|A380]] but was wary of having two major modification programs simultaneously.<ref name=AW140217/>

In March 2014, [[Delta Air Lines]] expressed an interest in the A330neo to replace its ageing, 20+-year-old [[Boeing 767-300ER]] jets.<ref name=AW140311/> In the 250-300-seat market, [[CIT Group]] believed an A330neo enables profitability on shorter ranges where the longer-range A350 and Boeing 787 are not optimised. CIT said that the A350-800 was not as efficient as it would like, and [[Air Lease Corporation|Air Lease Corp.]] added that the company did not consider it reasonable to take the A350-800 and A330neo as they saw no sustainable coexistence of the two aircraft.<ref name=AW140324/>

[[AirAsia X]] ended flights to London and Paris from Kuala Lumpur in 2012 because their Airbus A340s were not fuel-efficient enough and would try again with A330s.<ref name=WSJ140529/> As Airbus gradually increased the output of the new A350, prolonging the production run of the A330 could help to maintain profitability.<ref name=reuters140610/> After [[Emirates (airline)|Emirates]] cancelled 70 orders for the A350, Airbus said it continued to work on re-engining the smaller A330.<ref name=reuters140611/>

===Launch===
[[File:Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 tested at Arnold Air Force Base Engineering Development Complex.jpg|thumb|The [[Rolls-Royce Trent 7000]] being tested at [[Arnold Engineering Development Complex]]]]

<!--14 July 2014 -->
On 14 July 2014 at the [[Farnborough Airshow]], Airbus launched the A330neo programme, to be powered by the new [[Rolls-Royce Trent 7000]]. It would improve the [[Fuel economy in aircraft|fuel burn per seat]] by 14%. Airbus hoped to sell 1,000 A330neo aircraft. Its range would increase by {{convert|400|nmi}} and although 95% of the parts would be common with the A330ceo, maintenance costs would be lower. New [[winglet]]s, 3.7 metres wider and similar to those of the [[A350 XWB]], still within [[ICAO]] category E airport requirements, along with new engine pylons, would improve aerodynamics by 4%.<ref name=140714PR-living/>

The A330neo's development costs, an estimated $2 billion (£1.18 billion)<ref name=reuters140610/><!-- this estimation is consistent with Airbus' 0.7% of its €64.45Bn 2015 revenue = €451 million * 3 years = €1.35Bn --> , were expected to have an impact of around −0.7% on Airbus's [[return on sales]] target from 2015 to 2017.<ref name=140714PR-launch/> Airbus stated that lower [[capital cost]] would make the A330neo the most cost-efficient medium-range wide-body airliner.<ref name=140714PR-powering/> Airbus said that it could pursue demand for 4,000 aircraft and that there was an open market for 2,600 jets not already addressed by backlogs with operators already using A330s. Aerodynamic modifications would include a re-twisted wing and optimised [[Leading-edge slat|slats]].<ref name=FG140714/>

In 2014, ''[[The Airline Monitor]]'''s Ed Greenslet stated that the A330neo would have the advantage of not being designed to fly {{cvt|8,000|nmi|mi}}, unlike the A350 and Boeing 787 which were thus less economical on shorter routes, although "the vast majority of long-haul markets is 4,000 nmi or less".<!--<ref name=AW140714/>--> 
He also believed that an "A330neo would enjoy a monopoly in its segment instantly", with the [[Boeing 767]] "essentially out of production", the [[Boeing 757]] not replaced while the [[A321neo]] and the [[737-9]] are smaller and had less range, <!--<ref name=AW140714/>--> and that launching the A330neo would probably kill the smallest A350-800.<ref name=AW140714/>

John Leahy estimated that the A330-900 would have operating costs on par with the [[787-9]], but would be available at 25% lower capital costs and could reach a production rate of 10 per month after a 7/8 per month rate at the production start.<ref name=AW140716/> Both A330neo variants were expected to have a maximum take-off weight of 242 t. The type design was frozen in late 2015.<ref name=WSJ140716/>

[[Boeing]] Vice Chairman and Commercial Airplanes CEO [[Ray Conner]] dismissed the A330neo as 2004 revamp which cannot match the 787's direct [[operating costs]], being {{convert|20,000|lb|t|0|order=flip|spell=in}} heavier and having a wing only slightly improved from the 1980s design, and claimed the 787-10 was almost 30% more [[fuel economy in aircraft|efficient]] per-seat than the previous A330-300 and that a new engine would not close the gap – but he acknowledged that it could be a threat as it put pressure on Boeing as it sought to [[break even]] after 850–1,000 787 deliveries.<ref name=AW140721/>

=== Production ===
[[File:TAP Portugal A330neo interior ITB 2017.JPG|thumb|TAP Air Portugal interior mockup at [[ITB Berlin]] 2017]]

On 7 September 2015, Airbus announced that it had begun production of the first A330neo with the construction of its centre [[wingbox]] and engine pylon.<ref name=150907PR/> Final assembly of the first aircraft, an A330-900, started in September 2016 at the [[Airbus Toulouse]] site with the joining of the wings to the centre fuselage at the station 40.<ref name=160927PR/> In December 2016, the programme schedule slipped by six weeks due to marginal engine development at [[Rolls-Royce Holdings|Rolls-Royce]], and launch customer [[TAP Air Portugal]] projected its first A330neo would be delivered in March 2018.<ref name=reuters161216/>

The first aircraft left the paint shop in December 2016, awaiting its engines.<ref>{{Cite tweet |number=812325202474496002 |title=The #A330neo with its nice dress on! This new player offers −14% fuel burn/seat as well as the #AirspaceByAirbus cabin for ultimate comfort. |author= Airbus |user=Airbus |date=23 December 2016 }}</ref> By April 2017, the Trent 7000s were to be installed later during the summer so that the first flight was delayed until September.<ref name=FG170424/>
Due to the delay, TAP Air Portugal was not expected to receive the first A330neo until the end of the first half of 2018, or even in the third quarter.<ref name=Flight23may2017>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/tap-a330neo-deliveries-at-least-a-year-away-pinto-437522/ |title= TAP A330neo deliveries at least a year away: Pinto |date= 23 May 2017 |work= FlightGlobal |access-date= 23 May 2017 |archive-date= 19 August 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190819122926/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/tap-a330neo-deliveries-at-least-a-year-away-pinto-437522/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
The engines were shipped to Airbus in June.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/rolls-royce-sends-first-trent-7000-pair-to-airbus-438289/ |author-first1= Michael |author-last1=Gubisch |work= Flightglobal |title= Rolls-Royce sends first Trent 7000 pair to Airbus |date= 16 June 2017}}</ref> The aircraft complete with engines showed at Toulouse in September before its first flight.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://actu-aero.fr/2017/09/15/le-1er-airbus-a330neo-fait-son-roll-out-a-toulouse-blagnac/ |title= Le 1er Airbus A330neo fait son "roll-out" à Toulouse-Blagnac |date= 15 September 2017 |work= Actualité Aéronautique Francophone |language= fr |access-date= 16 September 2017 |archive-date= 16 September 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170916140800/https://actu-aero.fr/2017/09/15/le-1er-airbus-a330neo-fait-son-roll-out-a-toulouse-blagnac/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

Major structures of the first A330-800 were entering production in October 2017: [[high-lift device]]s are installed on the wing in [[Bremen]], fuselage sections are built in [[Hamburg]], the centre wing-box in [[Nantes]], titanium engine pylons in [[Toulouse]] and sharklet [[wingtip]]s in [[Korea]].<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-aims-for-first-a330-800-final-assembly-by-yea-441894/ |title= Airbus aims for first A330-800 final assembly by year-end |date= 6 October 2017 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 6 October 2017 |archive-date= 6 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171006121739/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-aims-for-first-a330-800-final-assembly-by-yea-441894/ |url-status= live }}</ref> Its final assembly started in November 2017, on track for its planned first flight in mid-2018.<ref name=Airbus29nov2017>{{cite press release |url= http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2017/11/new-a330-800-starts-final-assembly.html |date= 29 November 2017 |title= New A330-800 starts final assembly |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 29 November 2017 |archive-date= 1 December 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171201044001/http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2017/11/new-a330-800-starts-final-assembly.html |url-status= live }}</ref>
Structural assembly was completed by February 2018, having its flight-test instruments installed and waiting for its engines before its 300h flight-test programme.<!--<ref name=Flight1feb2018>-->
At this time, production aircraft progressed through the final assembly line with the first 'Airspace' cabin interior being fitted.<ref name=Flight1feb2018>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/picture-a330-800-closer-to-joining-a330neo-test-fle-445438/ |title= A330-800 closer to joining A330neo test fleet |date= 1 February 2018 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 2 February 2018 |archive-date= 2 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180202190333/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/picture-a330-800-closer-to-joining-a330neo-test-fle-445438/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

A330 production was cut to 50 deliveries in 2019, with more than half of them re-engined A330neos.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/over-half-of-a330-output-next-year-to-be-a330neos-448172/ |title= Over half of A330 output next year to be A330neos |date= 30 April 2018 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 3 May 2018 |archive-date= 4 May 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180504011723/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/over-half-of-a330-output-next-year-to-be-a330neos-448172/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
In April 2020, the production rate decreased from 3.5 to 2 per month due to the [[impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on aviation]], and finished planes were stored while waiting for deferred deliveries.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-not-expecting-significant-changes-in-production-rates-faury/139072.article |title= Airbus not expecting significant changes in production rates: Faury |author-first1= David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date= 30 June 2020 |work= FlightGlobal |access-date= 19 August 2020 |archive-date= 16 September 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200916090709/https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-not-expecting-significant-changes-in-production-rates-faury/139072.article |url-status= live }}</ref>
In 2018, unit cost was US$259.9 M for a -800 and US$296.4 M for a -900.<ref name="Airbus average list prices 2018"/>

=== Flight testing ===
[[File:Airbus A330neo First Flight crew.jpg|thumb|The first flight crew]]

The A330-900 first flight on 19 October 2017 was a debut of the 1,400 hours [[flight test]] campaign involving three prototypes plus the first production aircraft: 1,100 flight hours for the A330-900 and 300 flight hours for the A330-800, targeting mid-2018 EASA and FAA Type Certification.<ref name=Airbus19oct2017>{{cite press release |url= http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2017/10/first-a330neo-becomes-airborne-for-its-maiden-flight2.html |date= 19 October 2017 |title= First A330neo becomes airborne for its maiden flight |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171019201119/http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2017/10/first-a330neo-becomes-airborne-for-its-maiden-flight2.html |url-status= live }}</ref> The 4h 15m flight reached {{cvt|30,125|ft}} and {{cvt|502|knots|mph km/h}}.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.flightradar24.com/data/aircraft/f-wttn#f41b6f5 |title= F-WTTN - Airbus A330-941 - Airbus |work= Flightradar24 |date= 19 October 2017 |access-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171019220235/https://www.flightradar24.com/data/aircraft/f-wttn#f41b6f5 |url-status= live }}</ref> It should establish certain maximum [[operating point]]s and achieve an initial [[handling qualities]] assessment including at high [[angle of attack]].<!--<ref name=Flight19oct2017/>--> This first aircraft, MSN1795, was scheduled to perform 600 h and was to be joined the following month by the second, MSN1813, which will fly 500 h, before the third, MSN1819, the first customer aircraft for TAP Portugal with a complete cabin.<ref name=Flight19oct2017>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-starts-opening-a330neo-flight-envelope-442320/ |title= Airbus starts opening A330neo flight envelope |date= 19 October 2017 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171019160403/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-starts-opening-a330neo-flight-envelope-442320/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

Two [[flight test engineer]]s and two [[Flight mechanic|engine specialists]] monitored the 60GB per hour output of 1,375 sensors and 98,000 parameters, including strips of [[microelectromechanical systems]] to measure aerodynamic pressure distribution across the wing.<!--<ref name=Flight26oct2017/>--> MSN1795 was to undertake simulated icing tests and cold-weather tests in Canada, [[aircraft noise|noise]] assessment, [[autoland]] testing and high [[angle-of-attack]], minimum-unstick checks during [[Rotation (aeronautics)|rotation]] with a tail bumper.<!--<ref name=Flight26oct2017/>--> MSN1813 was to test natural [[icing conditions]], assess [[hot and high]] conditions in the [[United Arab Emirates]] and [[La Paz]], and fly 150h of route-proving; it has rakes and pressure sensors in the engine flows to compare actual [[thrust]] with ground bench measurements.<!--<ref name=Flight26oct2017/>--> MSN1819 was to validate the Airspace cabin interior fitting with artificial passengers for ventilation analysis and cabin environment measurements.<ref name=Flight26oct2017>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-a330-900-finally-embarks-on-flight-test-pr-442438/ |title= A330-900 finally embarks on flight-test programme |date= 26 October 2017 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 26 October 2017 |archive-date= 26 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171026131600/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-a330-900-finally-embarks-on-flight-test-pr-442438/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

The second test aircraft made its maiden flight on 4 December, to be used to validate aerodynamic & engine performance and airline operations.<ref>{{cite tweet |user= Airbus |number= 937634484421263361 |date= 4 December 2017 |title= Here's our 2nd A330neo test aircraft on its maiden flight. }}</ref>
By the end of January 2018, the first logged almost 200h in 58 flights while the second had accumulated nearly 120h in 30 flights.<!--<ref name=Flight1feb2018/>-->
Its [[flight envelope]] was fully opened including [[Flutter (aircraft)|flutter]] and [[aircraft stall|stall]] tests to complete powerplant calibration and [[Strake (aeronautics)|strake]] configuration has been frozen.<!--<ref name=Flight1feb2018/>-->
Airbus commenced [[autopilot]], [[autoland]] and high-speed performance testing, and was to move on to hot- and cold-weather tests, as well as noise and icing tests, over the following three months.<ref name=Flight1feb2018/> 
As of 10 April 2018, the two test aircraft had logged over 200 flights and more than 700 hours, testing −27 °C [[cold]] weather, natural [[Icing conditions|icing]], [[crosswind landing]], 37 °C and {{cvt|8,000|ft}} [[hot and high]] operations.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/news/en/2018/04/airbus--a330neo-continues-toward-its-2018-service-entry.html |date= 13 April 2018 |title= Airbus' A330neo continues toward its 2018 service entry |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 14 April 2018 |archive-date= 14 April 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180414172222/http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/news/en/2018/04/airbus--a330neo-continues-toward-its-2018-service-entry.html |url-status= live }}</ref>

The first [[TAP Air Portugal]] aircraft made its first flight on 15 May 2018; it joined the two previous test aircraft to check the [[aircraft cabin|cabin]] systems: [[Air conditioning pack|air conditioning]], [[crew rest]], etc.<ref name=Airbus15may2018>{{cite press release |url= http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2018/05/launch-operator-a330neo-completes-maiden-flight.html |date= 15 May 2018 |title= Launch operator A330neo completes maiden flight |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 16 May 2018 |archive-date= 16 May 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180516174227/http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2018/05/launch-operator-a330neo-completes-maiden-flight.html |url-status= live }}</ref> 
It started the final certification step on 18 June: function and reliability tests or route proving, including [[ETOPS]], [[diversion airport]] landing, and testing [[ground handling]] over 150 flight test hours, as the flight test programme reached 1,000 hours.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2018/06/airbus-a330neo-en-route-to-function---reliability-tests.html |title= Airbus A330neo en route to function and reliability tests |date= 18 June 2018 |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 19 June 2018 |archive-date= 19 June 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180619112927/http://www.airbus.com/newsroom/press-releases/en/2018/06/airbus-a330neo-en-route-to-function---reliability-tests.html |url-status= live }}</ref>
Entry into service was planned for the third quarter of 2018 and [[ETOPS]] was to be approved in October for 330min.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/farnborough-approvals-near-for-a330neo-450224/ |title= Farnborough: Approvals near for A330neo |date= 16 July 2018 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 24 July 2018 |archive-date= 24 July 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180724123611/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/farnborough-approvals-near-for-a330neo-450224/ |url-status= live}}</ref>

[[EASA]] granted the A330-941 type certificate on 26 September 2018, with ETOPS not yet approved.<ref name="TCDSrev47">{{cite web |url= https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/TCDS%20EASA.A.004%20-%20Rev%2047%20-%2026.09.2018.pdf |title= Type certificate data sheet No. EASA.A.004 for Airbus A330, revision 47 |publisher= European Aviation Safety Agency |date= 26 September 2018|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180926205950/https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/TCDS%20EASA.A.004%20-%20Rev%2047%20-%2026.09.2018.pdf |archive-date= 26 September 2018 }}</ref> ETOPS 180 min was approved on 14 November, restricted to engines with fewer than 500 flight cycles.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a330-900-secures-etops-with-engine-life-restrictions-453844/ |title= A330-900 secures ETOPS with engine-life restrictions |date= 22 November 2018 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 22 November 2018 |archive-date= 23 January 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190123171909/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a330-900-secures-etops-with-engine-life-restrictions-453844/ |url-status= live }}</ref><ref name="TCDS">{{cite web |url= https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/TCDS-EASA.A.004%20-%20Rev%2048%20-%2022.11.2018.pdf |title= Type certificate data sheet No. EASA.A.004 for Airbus A330, revision 48 |publisher= European Aviation Safety Agency |date= 22 November 2018 |access-date= 22 November 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181122215735/https://www.easa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/dfu/TCDS-EASA.A.004%20-%20Rev%2048%20-%2022.11.2018.pdf |archive-date= 22 November 2018 |url-status= dead }}</ref> 
Airbus expects the [[FAA]] type certification with 180 min ETOPS by the end of 2018 and 330 min ETOPS in the first half of 2019.<ref name=AIN12oct2018>{{cite news |url= https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-10-12/tap-air-portugal-aims-december-eis-its-first-a330neo |title= TAP Air Portugal Aims for December EIS of Its First A330neo |author-first1= Cathy |author-last1=Buyck |date= 12 October 2018 |work= AIN online |access-date= 13 October 2018 |archive-date= 13 October 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181013172221/https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-10-12/tap-air-portugal-aims-december-eis-its-first-a330neo |url-status= live }}</ref>
Beyond-180min ETOPS was approved by the EASA on 24 January 2019.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a330-900-secures-beyond-180min-etops-approval-455288/ |title= A330-900 secures beyond-180min ETOPS approval |date= 25 January 2019 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 25 January 2019 |archive-date= 25 January 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190125183631/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a330-900-secures-beyond-180min-etops-approval-455288/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

TAP made its first commercial flight on 15 December from [[Lisbon Airport|Lisbon]] to [[São Paulo–Guarulhos International Airport|São Paulo]].<ref name="TAP15dec2018" /> The airline should receive 15 more A330neos in 2019 and fly the A330-900 from Lisbon to [[Chicago O'Hare]] and [[Washington Dulles]] from June 2019, both five times a week.<ref name=Flight29nov2018>{{cite news|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/tap-takes-a330neo-to-chicago-and-washington-in-2019-454029/|title=TAP takes A330neo to Chicago and Washington in 2019|last=Russell|first=Edward|date=29 November 2018|work=[[FlightGlobal]]|access-date=27 December 2018|archive-date=27 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181227181654/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/tap-takes-a330neo-to-chicago-and-washington-in-2019-454029/|url-status=live}}</ref>

On the occasion of the 19 October 2017 first flight, an increase to {{cvt|251|t|lb}} [[MTOW]] by mid-2020 was announced, with a few changes to the landing gear and brakes, increasing its range by {{cvt|700|or|1000|nmi|mi km}} compared to the current A330neo or A330ceo.<ref name=ATW19oct2017>{{cite news |url= http://atwonline.com/airframes/airbus-a330neo-launches-first-flight-over-france |title= Airbus A330neo launches first flight over France |date= 19 October 2017 |author-first1= Kurt |author-last1=Hofmann |work= Aviation Week Network |access-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-date= 30 January 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180130084048/http://atwonline.com/airframes/airbus-a330neo-launches-first-flight-over-france |url-status= live }}</ref>
The 251 t MTOW was confirmed by Airbus in November 2017.<ref name=Airbus29nov2017/>
This gave the -900 a range of {{cvt|7200|nmi|mi km}} and {{cvt|8150|nmi|mi km}} for the -800.<ref name=Leeham20march2018>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2018/03/20/airbus-launches-the-longest-range-widebody-in-the-below-300-seat-market/ |title= Airbus launches the longest range widebody in the below 300 seat market |author-first1= Bjorn |author-last1=Fehrm |date= 20 March 2018 |work= Leeham News |access-date= 21 March 2018 |archive-date= 24 November 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181124105825/https://leehamnews.com/2018/03/20/airbus-launches-the-longest-range-widebody-in-the-below-300-seat-market/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
Test flights of the 251 t A330-900 started from 28 February 2020.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-carries-out-first-flight-of-251t-a330neo/137005.article |title= Airbus carries out first flight of 251t A330neo |author-first1= David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date= 28 February 2020 |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 28 February 2020 |archive-date= 28 February 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200228143933/https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-carries-out-first-flight-of-251t-a330neo/137005.article |url-status= live }}</ref>

The heavier structure allows a transpacific range and is balanced by a weight-reduction effort, keeping the same empty weight and payload.<ref name=Flight3mar2020>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-aims-for-short-test-campaign-on-251t-a330-900/137058.article |title= Airbus aims for short test campaign on 251t A330-900 |author-first1= David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date= 3 March 2020 |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 4 March 2020 |archive-date= 4 March 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200304063610/https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-aims-for-short-test-campaign-on-251t-a330-900/137058.article |url-status= live }}</ref>

Retaining 99% spares [[commonality]], it offers {{cvt|6|t|lb}} more payload while strengthening the landing-gear and extending the [[time before overhaul]] interval from 10 to 12 years.<ref name=Flight8oct2020>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/higher-weight-a330-900-secures-european-certification/140532.article |title= Higher-weight A330-900 secures European certification |author-first1= David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date= 8 October 2020 |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 9 October 2020 |archive-date= 19 October 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201019152958/https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/higher-weight-a330-900-secures-european-certification/140532.article |url-status= live }}</ref>
On 31 March 2021, Corsair took delivery of the first 251t Airbus A330-900 in a three-class, 352-seat configuration.<ref name=Flight31mar2021>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/fleets/corsair-fleet-renewal-begins-as-it-takes-first-higher-weight-airbus-a330neo/143135.article |title= Corsair fleet renewal begins as it takes first higher-weight Airbus A330neo |author-first1= Graham |author-last1=Dunn |date= 31 March 2021 |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 1 April 2021 |archive-date= 1 April 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210401124318/https://www.flightglobal.com/fleets/corsair-fleet-renewal-begins-as-it-takes-first-higher-weight-airbus-a330neo/143135.article |url-status= live }}</ref>
The 251 t A330-800 was certified by EASA in April 2022.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kaminski-Morrow |first1=David |title=EASA certifies A330-800 with 251t take-off weight |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/easa-certifies-a330-800-with-251t-take-off-weight/148282.article |work=Flight Global |date=14 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

On 11 June 2025, Airbus planned for 2028 a {{cvt|253|t|lb}} variant, while a 68,000 lbf (320 kN) thrust rating should be available from 2026.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/air-transport/airbus-to-enhance-a330neo-capability-with-further-take-off-weight-increase/163353.article |title= Airbus to enhance A330neo capability with further take-off weight increase |author-first1= David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date= 13 June 2025 |work= FlightGlobal}}</ref>

==Design==
[[File:Airbus A330neo, new sharklets.jpg|thumb|A350-inspired Sharklets]]

The A330neo is advertised as having a 12% fuel burn advantage per flight over the older A330 variants. This advantage comes from the 11% gain from the [[Rolls-Royce Trent 7000|Trent 7000]] and its larger 112-inch fan, compared to the 97.5-inch [[Rolls-Royce Trent 700|Trent 700]] engine. However, this gain is negated by 3%–2% by additional weight, and 1% due to engine drag, but the sharklets and aero optimization regain 4%, restoring the advantage to 12%. Furthermore, fuel consumption per seat is improved by 2% due to the rearranged cabin (Space-Flex and Smart-Lav) with increased seating, offering a 14% fuel burn reduction per seat for the new −900 compared to the previous 235-tonne −300 version.<ref name=LeahyPres/> The newer 242-tonne −300 is already 2% more efficient.<ref name=AW120709/>

Since the fan is enlarged from {{cvt|97|to|112|inch|cm}}, the [[nacelle]]s are mounted higher, necessitating extensive [[CFD analysis]] to avoid supersonic shock wave [[interference drag]], as is the first [[Leading-edge slat|slat]]'s dog-tooth.<!--<ref name=Leeham20oct2017/>--> The [[wing twist]] and belly [[aircraft fairing|fairing]]s are tweaked to approach the lowest drag elliptical span-wise [[pressure distribution]] changed by the larger sharklets, like the [[Flap (aeronautics)|flap]] [[Aircraft fairing|track fairings]] shape to lower [[form drag]].<ref name="Leeham20oct2017">{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2017/10/20/bjorns-corner-airbus-a330neo-flight-test-starts/ |title= Bjorn's Corner: Airbus A330neo flight test starts |author-first1= Bjorn |author-last1=Fehrm |date= 20 October 2017 |work= Leeham |access-date= 20 October 2017 |archive-date= 23 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180223145201/https://leehamnews.com/2017/10/20/bjorns-corner-airbus-a330neo-flight-test-starts/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

Initially based on the largest 242t MTOW A330, Airbus was studying an improvement to {{convert|245|t|lbs|abbr=on}} MTOW for the A330neo, which would match the figure originally given for the [[Airbus A350-800]] before it was sidelined in favor of the A330neo.<ref name="FG160531" /> This would give the -900 a {{cvt|7,000|nmi|0}} range to better compete with the [[787-9]]’s {{cvt|7,635|nmi}}<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2017/09/28/airbus-working-7000nm-a330-900neo/ |title= Airbus is working on a 7,000nmi A330-900 |author-first1= Bjorn |author-last1=Fehrm |date= 28 September 2017 |work= Leeham |access-date= 28 September 2017 |archive-date= 21 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180221183027/https://leehamnews.com/2017/09/28/airbus-working-7000nm-a330-900neo/ |url-status= live }}</ref> On the -800 at FL400, cruise fuel flow at Mach 0.82 and low weight is {{cvt|4.7 to 5.2|t|lb}} per hour at a higher weight and Mach 0.83.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://aviationweek.com/a330neo |title= Pilot Report: There's More To A330neo Than Reengining |date= 2 May 2019 |author-first1= Tim |author-last1=Wuerfel |work= Aviation Week & Space Technology}}</ref>

=== Engines ===
[[File:TAP A330-900NEO just arrived at Lisbon airport (40589888703) (cropped).jpg|thumb|The Trent 7000 on-wing]]

Candidate engines included variants of Rolls-Royce's Trent 1000 and General Electric's [[General Electric GEnx|GEnx-1B]]. Both engine makers were reportedly interested in winning an exclusive deal should a [[re-engine]]d A330 be offered. The Trent 1000 TEN (Thrust, Efficiency, New Technology) engine was under development for the 787-10, but Rolls-Royce intended to offer a broad power range.<ref name=AW140131/>

The A330neo uses the [[Rolls-Royce Trent 7000]] engine, which is an electronic controlled [[bleed air]] variant of the [[Rolls-Royce Trent 1000|Trent 1000]] used on the [[Boeing 787-10]].<!--<ref name=Trent7000/>--> It will have a {{convert|112|in|cm|0|abbr=on}} diameter fan and a 10:1 bypass ratio.<ref name=140714PR-powering/> Variants deliver thrusts of {{convert|68000|to|72,000|lbf|kN}}.<ref name=Trent7000/>

The Trent is the exclusive powerplant, as Rolls-Royce offered better terms to obtain exclusivity. Customers bemoan the loss of competition among engine makers: [[Steven Udvar-Hazy]], CEO of [[Air Lease Corporation]], said that he wants a choice of engines, but Airbus has pointed out that equipping a commercial aircraft to handle more than one type of engine adds several hundred million dollars to the development cost. The head of [[Pratt and Whitney]] said: "Engines are no longer commodities...the optimization of the engine and the aircraft becomes more relevant."<ref name=WSJ140716/>

The decision to offer the aircraft with only one engine option is not unique to Airbus; the [[Boeing 777X]] will come equipped exclusively with [[General Electric GE9X]] engines, after Rolls-Royce made a bid with its [[Rolls-Royce Trent#Research|Advance]] configuration but was not selected.<ref name=AW130318/>

==Variants==
===A330-800===
[[File:9K-APF Airbus A330-841 Kuwait Airways Frankfurt 22.6.22.jpg|thumb|The A330-800 was introduced by [[Kuwait Airways]] on 20 November 2020.]]

The A330-800 retains the fuselage length of the [[A330-200]], but can seat six more passengers (for a total of 252) with an optimised cabin featuring 18-inch-wide economy seats.<ref name=140714PR-living/> The -800 has a range of 8,100 nmi (15,000 km; {{cvt|8100|nmi|mi|disp=output only}}) with 257 passengers (406 max).<ref name="Airbus Family figures"/>
As the variants share 99% [[commonality]], developing the smaller -800 has a negligible extra cost.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-06-18/airbus-a330neo-en-route-function-and-reliability-tests |title= Airbus A330neo En Route to Function and Reliability Tests |author-first= Gregory |author-last1=Polek |date= 18 June 2018 |work= AIN online |access-date= 19 June 2018 |archive-date= 19 June 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180619113043/https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2018-06-18/airbus-a330neo-en-route-function-and-reliability-tests |url-status= live }}</ref>

After the first flight of the -900 on 19 October 2017, Hawaiian Airlines (then the only customer for the -800) considered changing its order to six -800s, seeking best to fit its current network to Asia and North America whilst allowing for future growth, possibly to Europe.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiian-seeking-a330-800neo-alternatives-ceo-442337/ |title= Hawaiian seeking A330-800neo alternatives: CEO |date= 19 October 2017 |author-first1= Jon |author-last1=Hemmerdinger |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 20 October 2017 |archive-date= 20 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171020181051/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiian-seeking-a330-800neo-alternatives-ceo-442337/ |url-status= live }}</ref> Demand for the -800 fell to 3%. In contrast, the -200 commanded 40% of the CEO deliveries: its range advantage has eroded with the increased capabilities of the -900, and although it offers lower fuel use per trip, fuel use per seat is higher.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2017/11/02/airbus-a330-800-not-selling/ |title= Why is Airbus A330-800 not selling? |author-first1= Bjorn |author-last1=Fehrm |date= 2 November 2017 |work= Leeham}}</ref>

As of 2017, demand for the -800 was limited by low fuel prices and the -200s it might replace after 2020 were still young (nine years on average). The [[Boeing 767-300]]s that the -800 might replace are 15 years older, and while Boeing considered relaunching production of the [[Boeing 767|767-300ER]], mainly as an interim for American and United Airlines, this was complicated by a 30-year-old design including obsolete cabin amenities.<!--<ref name=Leeham6Dec2017/>--> At this time, Boeing intended to launch its [[Boeing New Midsize Airplane|New Midsize Airplane]] no earlier than 2027, affording Airbus opportunities with the 95 operators of the A330ceo. Long-haul [[low-cost carrier]]s were a target for high-density nine-abreast layouts for 386 seats over {{cvt|6,000|-|6,500|nmi}} at the {{cvt|251|t|lb}} MTOW, {{cvt|500|nmi}} more than a similarly loaded 787-8 and with up to 30 more seats.<ref name=Leeham6Dec2017>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2017/12/06/airbus-strategy-a330-800/ |title= Airbus' strategy for the A330-800 |author-first1= Scott |author-last1=Hamilton |date= 6 December 2017 |work= Leeham |access-date= 6 December 2017 |archive-date= 2 March 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180302195504/https://leehamnews.com/2017/12/06/airbus-strategy-a330-800/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

Production of the -800 beyond the prototype was in doubt, as Hawaiian was choosing between the [[Airbus A350-900]] and the [[Boeing 787]]-8/9.<ref name=Leeham6Dec2017/> In February 2018, Hawaiian was thought to be cancelling its order for six A330-800s, replacing them with Boeing 787-9s priced at less than $100–115m, close to their production cost of $80–90m, while [[Boeing Capital]] released Hawaiian from three 767-300ER leases well in advance.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2018/02/20/boeing-displaces-airbus-hawaiian-wins-787-9-deal-airline-cancels-a330-800-order/ |title= Boeing displaces Airbus at Hawaiian, wins 787-9 deal; airline cancels A330-800 order |date= 20 February 2018 |work= Leeham |access-date= 21 February 2018 |archive-date= 16 January 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200116073559/https://leehamnews.com/2018/02/20/boeing-displaces-airbus-hawaiian-wins-787-9-deal-airline-cancels-a330-800-order/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
Hawaiian denied that the order for the A330-800 had been cancelled, but did not dismiss a new deal with Boeing.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiians-a330-800-order-remains-in-place-for-now-446147/ |title= Hawaiian's A330-800 order remains in place, for now: airline |date= 22 February 2018 |author-first1= Jon |author-last1=Hemmerdinger |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 23 February 2018 |archive-date= 6 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190406202739/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiians-a330-800-order-remains-in-place-for-now-446147/ |url-status= live }}</ref> In March 2018, Hawaiian confirmed the cancellation of its order for six A330-800s and ordered ten B787-9s instead.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiian-signs-for-10-787-9s-and-cancels-a330-800-or-446506/ |title= Hawaiian signs for 10 787-9s and cancels A330-800 order |date= 6 March 2018 |author-first1= Jon |author-last1=Hemmerdinger |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 6 March 2018 |archive-date= 21 May 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190521100130/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/hawaiian-signs-for-10-787-9s-and-cancels-a330-800-or-446506/ |url-status= live }}</ref> Airbus says it was "simply undercut in price".<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-philosophical-over-loss-of-sole-a330-800-orde-446523/ |title= Airbus philosophical over loss of sole A330-800 order |date= 7 March 2018 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 7 March 2018 |archive-date= 7 March 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180307133151/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/airbus-philosophical-over-loss-of-sole-a330-800-orde-446523/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

===A330-900===
[[File:CS-TUR@PEK (20200411084804).jpg|thumb|The -900 retains the [[A330-300]] fuselage. TAP Air Portugal was the launch operator of this variant.]]

The A330-900 retains the fuselage length of the [[A330-300]] and [[A340-300]]. Cabin optimisation allows ten additional seats on the A330-900 (310 passengers) with 18-inch-wide economy seats.<ref name=140714PR-living/> The -900 travels 7,350 nmi (13,600 km; {{cvt|7350|nmi|mi|disp=output only}}) with 287 passengers (440 max).<ref name="Airbus Family figures"/>

[[Delta Air Lines|Delta]] expects a 20 percent reduction in operating cost per seat over the [[Boeing 767-300ER]] aircraft it replaces.<ref>{{cite news |title=Delta makes it official -- picks Airbus over Boeing |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/news/2014/11/20/delta-makes-it-official-picks-airbus-over-boeing.html |access-date=3 February 2020 |work=www.bizjournals.com |date=20 November 2014 |archive-date=7 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210307094207/https://www.bizjournals.com/atlanta/news/2014/11/20/delta-makes-it-official-picks-airbus-over-boeing.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Further reconfiguration of cabin facilities enables the –900 to seat up to 460 passengers in an all-economy layout.<ref name=460p>{{cite news |last1=Kaminski-Morrow |first1=David |title=Cebu Pacific to take 460-seat A330neos |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/paris-cebu-pacific-to-take-460-seat-a330neos-459076/ |work=Flightglobal |date=18 June 2019 |access-date=18 June 2019 |archive-date=18 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190618100754/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/paris-cebu-pacific-to-take-460-seat-a330neos-459076/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This exceeds the existing 440-seat maximum exit limit allowed by the type certificate, and requires a modification of the Type-A [[Emergency exit#Aircraft|exit door]]s to meet emergency exit requirements.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kaminski-Morrow |first1=David |title=Modified exit doors key to 460-seat Cebu A330neos |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/paris-modified-exit-doors-key-to-460-seat-cebu-a330-459203/ |work=Flightglobal |date=19 June 2019 |access-date=20 June 2019 |archive-date=20 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620074440/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/paris-modified-exit-doors-key-to-460-seat-cebu-a330-459203/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
In November 2019, maximum accommodation increased to 460 seats, through the installation of new 'Type-A+' [[Emergency exit#Aircraft|exits]], with a dual-lane evacuation slide.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a350-1000-maximum-seating-rises-to-480-462615/ |title= A350-1000 maximum seating rises to 480 |date= 29 Nov 2019 |first= David |last= Kaminski-Morrow |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 30 November 2019 |archive-date= 30 November 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20191130154202/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a350-1000-maximum-seating-rises-to-480-462615/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Freighter ===
[[Amazon Air]] and [[UPS Airlines]] pushed for a [[cargo aircraft|freighter]] version, stretching the A330-900 to carry more cargo over a shorter range, but it competes with the cheaper option of converting readily available retired passenger 767 and A330 aircraft.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-03-19/airbus-is-said-to-weigh-new-a330-cargo-model-spurred-by-amazon | title=Airbus Weighs New A330 Cargo Model, Spurred by Amazon | work=bloomberg.com | date=19 March 2018 | agency=Bloomberg | access-date=20 March 2018 | archive-date=20 March 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180320024050/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-03-19/airbus-is-said-to-weigh-new-a330-cargo-model-spurred-by-amazon | url-status=live }}</ref>
Development costs for the proposed freighter would be lower than for a new program, as much of the engineering has already been done for the A330-200F.<ref>{{cite news |work= Cargo Facts |title= The next big freighter? |author-first1= David |author-last1=Harris |date= March 22, 2018 |url= https://cargofacts.com/allposts/equipment/aircraft/the-next-big-freighter/ |access-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-date= 1 March 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200301173314/https://cargofacts.com/allposts/equipment/aircraft/the-next-big-freighter/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

=== Military ===
Airbus formally launched the tanker variant of the A330neo, dubbed as the A330 MRTT+, at the 2024 [[Farnborough International Airshow]]. The A330 MRTT+ is based on the A330-800 and is intended to replace the [[Airbus A330 MRTT|A330 MRTT]]. The A330 MRTT+ also retains the {{Convert|111000|kg|lb|abbr=on}} fuel capacity of the A330 MRTT.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://aviationweek.com/defense-space/multi-mission-aircraft/airbus-develop-second-generation-mrtt-based-a330neo|title=Airbus Sees MRTT+ In Customer Hands By 2030|author-first1=Robert |author-last1=Wall|date=24 July 2024|work=Aviation Week}}</ref> Airbus plans to deliver the first A330 MRTT+ in 2029.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://aviationweek.com/defense/aircraft-propulsion/airbus-planning-mrtt-neo-derived-mrtt-transition-2028|title=Airbus Planning MRTT To Neo-Derived MRTT+ Transition In 2028|author-first1=Tony |author-last1=Osborne|date=17 June 2025|work=Aviation Week}}</ref> The launch customer is expected to be the [[Royal Thai Air Force]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-09-25 |title=Royal Thai Air Force has ordered Airbus A330 MRTT+ {{!}} Airbus |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-09-royal-thai-air-force-orders-next-generation-airbus-a330-mrtt |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=www.airbus.com |language=en}}</ref>

{{See also|List of Airbus A330 operators}}
[[File:Delta Airbus A330-900 N415DX departing Boston June 2025 1.jpg|alt=[[Delta Air Lines|Delta]]'s A330-900neo in flight|thumb|right|[[Delta Air Lines]] is the largest operator of the A330neo.]]

There are 203 aircraft in service with 25 operators {{as of|2026|10|lc=y}}.
The five largest operators of A330neo are [[Delta Air Lines]] (39), [[TAP Air Portugal]] (19), [[Condor (airline)|Condor]] (18), [[ITA Airways]] (17) and [[Cebu Pacific]] (15).<ref name="Airbus_O_D" />

On 11 April 2023, Airbus delivered the 100th A330neo, an A330-900, to German airline [[Condor (airline)|Condor Flugdienst GmbH]], which would lease it from AerCap. At that time, the A330neo Family flew in the liveries of 22 airlines on over 200 routes and destinations worldwide.<ref name= 100thdeliver>{{cite press release |date=11 April 2023 |title=Flying towards a promising future; Airbus delivers its 100th A330neo |url=https://aircraft.airbus.com/en/newsroom/stories/2023-04-flying-towards-a-promising-future |publisher= Airbus |access-date=16 April 2023}}</ref>

===Market===
[[File:N361HA & JA835J @ HNL, 2019-03-23.jpg|thumb|A [[Japan Airlines]] [[787-8]] alongside a [[Hawaiian Airlines|Hawaiian]] [[A330-200]] in [[Honolulu Airport|Honolulu]].]]
Third party analysis for a {{cvt|3350|nmi}} [[transatlantic flight]] shows that the [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner|787-9]] has a slight advantage over the A330-900 in cash cost per [[available seat miles]], while the Airbus outperforms the Boeing once capital costs are included, based on the A330-900 cost an estimated $10.6m less.<!-- $260M/25 A330-900 --><ref name=AN141125/>
They have close economics but the A330neo costs up to $30m less, according to another publication.<ref name=Wave>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2018/03/06/retirement-wave-coming-will-boost-a330neo-sales-says-airbus/ |title= Retirement wave coming that will boost A330neo sales, says Airbus |date= 6 March 2018 |work= Leeham |access-date= 7 March 2018 |archive-date= 6 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190406180746/https://leehamnews.com/2018/03/06/retirement-wave-coming-will-boost-a330neo-sales-says-airbus/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
An A330-900 is worth $115 million in 2018, while a new B787-9 valuation is $145 million, up from $135 million in 2014, but it may have been sold for $110–$115 million to prevent A330neo sales.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.aircraftvaluenews.com/intense-a330b787-competition-could-impact-values/ | title=Intense A330/B787 Competition Could Impact Values | work=aircraftvaluenews.com | date=11 June 2018 | author=Aircraft Value News | access-date=11 June 2018 | archive-date=12 June 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612143408/http://www.aircraftvaluenews.com/intense-a330b787-competition-could-impact-values/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

Between the 2004 launch of the Dreamliner and the A330neo launch in 2014, the market was split almost equally between both, with between 900 and 920 A330ceos sold against 950 to 1,000 787-8/9s.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-can-airbus-challenge-787-with-a330neo-409962/ |title= Can Airbus challenge 787 with A330neo? |date= 23 March 2015 |author-first1= Max |author-last1=Kingsley-Jones |work= Flight |access-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-date= 19 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171019221403/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-can-airbus-challenge-787-with-a330neo-409962/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
Between 2014 and the neo first flight in October 2017, the A330/A330neo had 440 orders (excluding freighters) compared to 272 for the 787-8/9 (excluding the -10), or since the 787 launch, 1211 A330ceo/neos compared to 1106 787-8/9s.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.airbus.com/content/dam/corporate-topics/publications/backgrounders/A330neo-First-Flight-Commercial-Update.pdf |title= Powering into the future : A330neo First Flight |date= 19 October 2017 |author-first1= Crawford |author-last1=Hamilton - Head of A330 marketing |publisher= Airbus |access-date= 9 March 2018 |archive-date= 10 March 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180310074034/http://www.airbus.com/content/dam/corporate-topics/publications/backgrounders/A330neo-First-Flight-Commercial-Update.pdf |url-status= live }}</ref>
Teal Group's Richard Aboulafia believes that the A330neo should dominate the lower range and lower capacity end of the [[Widebody aircraft|twin aisle]] market because the 787-8 has the high operating economics and unit price associated with its 8,000-nm range.<ref name=AW160329/>

[[Flightglobal]] Ascend Consultancy forecast 600 deliveries including 10% of -800 variants, less optimistic than Airbus's 1,000.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-where-does-hawaiian-switch-leave-a330-800-446594/ |title= Where does Hawaiian switch leave A330-800? |date= 8 March 2018 |author-first1= Max |author-last1=Kingsley-Jones |work= Flightglobal |access-date= 9 March 2018 |archive-date= 10 March 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180310074009/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-where-does-hawaiian-switch-leave-a330-800-446594/ |url-status= live }}</ref>
At entry into service in 2018, sales were disappointing and [[A330]] production was to be cut to 50 in 2019 down from 67 in 2017: while it was the widebody with the largest operator base with 1,390 deliveries since 1993, the fleet was still very young with only 46 aircraft retired. Airbus believed A330 operators would start fleet renewal beginning in 2020.<ref name=Wave/> With the exception of [[Delta Air Lines|Delta]], industry-leading airlines preferred the Boeing 787.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/airbus-struggles-a330neo-sales-reduces-output |title= Airbus Struggles With A330neo Sales, Reduces Output |date= 7 May 2018 |author-first1= Jens |author-last1=Flottau |work= Aviation Week & Space Technology |access-date= 7 May 2018 |archive-date= 7 May 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180507042820/http://aviationweek.com/commercial-aviation/airbus-struggles-a330neo-sales-reduces-output |url-status= live }}</ref>

Between January 2014 and November 2019, the A330/A330neo had 477 net orders (net of cancellations) compared to a total of 407 for all three variants of the 787.<ref name=AW11122019>{{cite news |title=Widebody Market Weakness Shows Signs Of Permanent Structural Change |url=https://aviationweek.com/air-transport/widebody-market-weakness-shows-signs-permanent-structural-change |access-date=4 February 2020 |work=Aviation Week Network |date=11 December 2019 |archive-date=4 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204042151/https://aviationweek.com/air-transport/widebody-market-weakness-shows-signs-permanent-structural-change |url-status=live }}</ref> The A330neo program was the best-selling Airbus widebody over the same period.<ref name=AW11122019/>
Airbus believes there is potential for the A330neo in the growing long-haul, low-cost carrier sector.<ref name=Wave/> While Airbus expected a market for over 1,000 A330neos, one pessimistic forecast reported in 2018 came in as low as 400 sales, in that the A330neo was late to the market and fuel prices had declined markedly over the years, reducing demand. {{as of|2018|6|lc=n}}, 19% of A330 operators also operate the Boeing 787. Leeham News argued that the A330-800 does not fully cover the upper end of Boeing's studied [[Boeing New Midsize Airplane|New Midsize Airplane]] market, while also describing the A330-800 as a cost-effective entry for Airbus into the upper end of the [[middle of the market]].<ref>{{cite news |url= https://leehamnews.com/2018/06/06/airbus-sees-potential-for-a330neo-sales-boeing-sees-opportunity/ |title= Airbus sees potential for A330neo sales; Boeing sees opportunity |date= 6 June 2018 |work= Leeham News |access-date= 6 June 2018 |archive-date= 6 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190406180749/https://leehamnews.com/2018/06/06/airbus-sees-potential-for-a330neo-sales-boeing-sees-opportunity/ |url-status= live }}</ref> In May 2019, Airbus's chief commercial officer made clear the company has a “rock”, the A321neo, and a “hard place”, the A330-800, for any airframer intending to bring a new airplane into the middle of the market at a time when Boeing was mired in the [[Boeing 737 MAX groundings|737 MAX crisis]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Airbus has the "rock" and "hard place" for Boeing NMA |url=https://leehamnews.com/2019/05/21/airbus-has-the-rock-and-hard-place-for-boeing-nma/ |access-date=3 February 2020 |work=Leeham News and Analysis |date=21 May 2019 |archive-date=3 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203132513/https://leehamnews.com/2019/05/21/airbus-has-the-rock-and-hard-place-for-boeing-nma/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Compared to a 283-seat, 9-abreast 787-9, Airbus claims a 1% lower [[fuel economy in aircraft|fuel burn]] for the -900: 3% higher due to the {{cvt|4–5|t|lb}} higher [[Operating empty weight|OEW]], but 4% lower due to the {{cvt|4|m}} wider [[wingspan]], and 3% lower fuel burn per seat in a 287-seat, 8-abreast configuration, reaching 7% with a 303-seat, 9-abreast layout.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://airwaysmag.com/airlines/first-a330neo-delivery-tap/ |title=Airbus Delivers First A330neo To TAP Portugal |date=26 November 2018 |author-first1=Daniel |author-last1=Sander |author-first2=James |author-last2=Field |work=Airways International |access-date=26 November 2018 |archive-date=26 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181126174434/https://airwaysmag.com/airlines/first-a330neo-delivery-tap/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
